questions.question: Consider minimizing $Z=f_0(\boldsymbol{x})$ subject to $f_i(\boldsymbol{x})\leq b_i$ for $i=1,\dots,m$, where $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and every $f_i$ maps $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Under which condition is this a convex optimization problem?
options: When $f_0$ is convex, whatever the constraint functions $f_1,\dots,f_m$ are.
When the feasible region is convex, whatever the functions $f_0,\dots,f_m$ are.
When $f_0,f_1,\dots,f_m$ are all convex functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
When $f_0$ is convex and the constraint functions $f_1,\dots,f_m$ are concave.

questions.question: For a convex optimization problem minimize $f_0(\boldsymbol{x})$ subject to $f_i(\boldsymbol{x})\leq b_i$, $i=1,\dots,m$, with all $f_i\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ convex, which argument shows that the feasible region is convex?
options: Each set $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon f_i(\boldsymbol{x})\leq b_i\}$ is convex as a sublevel set of a convex function, and the region is their intersection.
Each set $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon f_i(\boldsymbol{x})\leq b_i\}$ is a sublevel set of a convex function, hence convex, and the region is their union.
Each convex $f_i$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^n$, so the region is closed, and a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is convex.
The objective $f_0$ is convex, and the feasible region is the set where $f_0$ is minimized, which is convex for a convex $f_0$.

questions.question: A convex optimization problem minimize $f_0(\boldsymbol{x})$ subject to $f_i(\boldsymbol{x})\leq b_i$ (all $f_i$ convex on $\mathbb{R}^n$) needs the extra equality $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=\beta$, with $\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{R}^n$, $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$. How can it be added so that the problem stays convex?
options: It cannot be added: an equality constraint always makes the feasible region non-convex.
As the single constraint $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\beta$, since it will be binding at an optimum anyway.
As the two constraints $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\beta$ and $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq-\beta$, whose functions are both affine.
As the two constraints $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\beta$ and $-\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq-\beta$, whose functions are affine.

questions.question: A linear program can be written as minimize $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i$, $i=1,\dots,m$, with $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$. How are linear programs related to convex optimization problems?
options: No linear program is a convex optimization problem, since affine functions are not strictly convex.
Every linear program is a convex optimization problem, since affine functions are convex.
A linear program is a convex optimization problem only when its feasible region is bounded.
A linear program is a convex optimization problem only when written in standard form with $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$.

questions.question: In a minimization problem with a convex objective, a modeller writes the constraint $g(\boldsymbol{x})\geq c$, where $g\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is convex but not affine. Which statement about this constraint is correct?
options: Written as $-g(\boldsymbol{x})\leq-c$, it has the required $\leq$ form, so the problem is a convex optimization problem.
Written as $-g(\boldsymbol{x})\leq-c$, the function $-g$ is concave and not convex, so the definition is not met.
The set $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon g(\boldsymbol{x})\geq c\}$ is never convex, whatever the value of the constant $c$.
The set $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon g(\boldsymbol{x})\geq c\}$ is convex, being the complement of the convex set $\{g<c\}$.

questions.question: The problem minimize $Z=(x_1-1)^2+x_2^2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq3$, $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2$, is a convex optimization problem. Which added constraint keeps it a convex optimization problem?

The problem maximize $Z=6x_1+2x_2-x_1^2-x_2^2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq2$ is rewritten as a minimization of the form minimize $f_0$ subject to $f_1(\boldsymbol{x})\leq b_1$. Which rewriting and conclusion are correct?
options: Minimize $x_1^2+x_2^2-6x_1-2x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq2$; convex, since this objective is convex.
Minimize $6x_1+2x_2-x_1^2-x_2^2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq2$; not convex, since this objective is concave.
Minimize $x_1^2+x_2^2-6x_1-2x_2$ subject to $-x_1-x_2\leq-2$; convex, since all functions are convex.
Minimize $x_1^2+x_2^2-6x_1-2x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq2$; not convex, since the original $Z$ is concave.

questions.question: A convex optimization problem in $\mathbb{R}^2$ has the constraints (i) $x_1^2+x_2^2\leq5$, (ii) $2x_1-x_2\leq3$ and (iii) $x_1+3x_2\geq4$. Which constraints are binding at the feasible point $(2,1)$?
options: All three, since $(2,1)$ satisfies each of them.
Only (iii), since it holds with strict inequality.
Constraints (i) and (ii), but not (iii).
None, since $(2,1)$ satisfies all three constraints.

questions.question: Consider minimize $Z=x_2$ subject to $\mathrm{e}^{x_1}-x_2\leq0$, $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2$. Which statement about this problem is correct?
options: It is convex, and $\boldsymbol{x}=(0,1)$ is optimal, since the constraint is binding there.
It is not convex, since its feasible region is unbounded, and so no optimum can be guaranteed.
It is convex, so it has an optimal solution, and the optimal value is $Z=0$.
It is convex but has no optimal solution: $Z$ gets arbitrarily close to $0$ but never equals $0$.

questions.question: The linear program minimize $Z=3x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+2x_2\geq4$, $x_1\geq0$, $x_2\geq0$ is written in the form minimize $f_0(\boldsymbol{x})$ subject to $f_i(\boldsymbol{x})\leq b_i$. Which list of constraints is correct?

Let $h\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex but not affine, and let $f_0$ be convex. Which statement about minimizing $f_0$ subject to the single equality constraint $h(\boldsymbol{x})=b$ is correct?
options: Splitting $h=b$ into $h\leq b$ and $-h\leq-b$ needs $-h$ convex, which fails; $\{h=b\}$ can be a circle.
It is a convex optimization problem, since $\{h=b\}$ is a subset of the convex sublevel set $\{h\leq b\}$.
The set $\{h=b\}$ is never convex, so no such problem can have a convex feasible region.
Equality constraints are always binding, and binding constraints are not allowed in a convex optimization problem.

questions.question: A modeller maximizes a convex, non-affine $f_0\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ subject to $f_i(\boldsymbol{x})\leq b_i$ with all $f_i$ convex, and calls it a convex optimization problem because every function involved is convex. Which statement is correct?
options: It is one, since maximizing and minimizing $f_0$ over this region share the same convex feasible region.
It is not one, since no maximization problem can be a convex optimization problem in the minimization form.
It is not one: as minimize $-f_0$ its objective is concave, not convex, and local maxima can fail to be global.
It is one provided $f_0$ is strictly convex, because the maximizer of a strictly convex function is unique.

questions.question: For a linear optimization problem whose feasible region has an extreme point, an optimal solution, if one exists, is attained at an extreme point. Which statement about a convex optimization problem with a nonlinear objective is correct?
options: Its optimal solutions still lie at extreme points, because its feasible region is convex like that of a linear program.
Its optimum can lie at a point that is not extreme, even inside the region, so checking extreme points can miss it.
It can have an optimal solution only when its feasible region has at least one extreme point.
Its optimal solution always lies on the boundary of the region, where at least one constraint is binding.

questions.question: Decide whether minimize $Z=|x_1|+2|x_2-1|$ subject to $\max\{x_1+x_2,\,x_1-x_2\}\leq3$, $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2$, is a convex optimization problem. Which verdict, with its reason, is correct?
options: It is not convex: its functions are not differentiable, so no positive semidefinite Hessian can show convexity.
It is convex only once the constraint is split into $x_1+x_2\leq3$ and $x_1-x_2\leq3$; a maximum cannot serve as $f_1$.
It is convex, and it stays convex with $\min\{x_1+x_2,\,x_1-x_2\}\leq3$, since a minimum of affine functions is affine.
It is convex: each absolute value is a maximum of two affine functions, and nonnegative sums and maxima keep convexity.

questions.question: Is minimize $Z=x_1+x_2^2$ subject to $x_1^2+x_2^2\leq1$ and $x_1+x_2\geq2$, $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2$, a convex optimization problem, and does it have an optimal solution?
options: It is not a convex problem: its feasible region is empty, and the empty set is not convex.
It is a convex problem with optimal solution $(1,1)$, the point of the line $x_1+x_2=2$ nearest the disc.
It is a convex problem with an empty feasible region, so it has no optimal solution.
It is convex, and the circle point $(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})$, closest to the halfplane, is optimal.

questions.question: For which values of the parameter $a\in\mathbb{R}$ is minimize $Z=x_1^2+ax_1x_2+4x_2^2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\geq1$ a convex optimization problem?
options: Exactly for $-4\leq a\leq4$
Exactly for $-4<a<4$
Exactly for $-8\leq a\leq8$
Exactly for $0\leq a\leq4$

questions.question: The problem minimize $Z=x^2$ subject to $4-x^2\leq0$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, has exactly two optimal solutions, $x=-2$ and $x=2$. Which statement about this problem is correct?
options: It is a convex optimization problem, since the objective $x^2$ is convex and the optimal value $4$ is attained.
It becomes a convex optimization problem after rewriting the constraint equivalently as $x^2\geq4$.
Its two optimal solutions show that the objective $x^2$ is not strictly convex on its feasible region.
No convex constraint functions can describe its region, as the optimal set for $x^2$ would then be convex.

questions.question: A convex optimization problem minimize $f_0(\boldsymbol{x})$ subject to $f_i(\boldsymbol{x})\leq b_i$, $i=1,\dots,m$, has an objective $f_0$ that is strictly convex on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Which list contains every possible number of optimal solutions, and no impossible one?
options: Exactly one, since a strictly convex objective has a unique minimizer on a convex region.
None or exactly one, since two optimal solutions would have a midpoint with a smaller value.
None, exactly one or infinitely many, since this holds for every convex optimization problem.
None or exactly one, where none happens only when the feasible region is empty.

questions.question: Consider minimize $Z=(x-3)^2$ subject to $x^3\leq8$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Which statement about this problem and its optimal solution is correct?
options: Not convex as written ($x^3$ is not convex), but convex with the equivalent $x\leq2$; $x=2$ is optimal.
Convex as written, since its feasible region $(-\infty,2]$ is convex; the optimal solution is $x=2$.
Not convex in any form, since the constraint function $x^3$ is not convex; the optimal solution is $x=2$.
Convex with the equivalent constraint $x\leq2$; the optimal solution is $x=3$, where $Z'=0$.

questions.question: Consider minimize $Z=x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1^2+x_2^2=2$, which is not a convex problem. Replacing the equality by $x_1^2+x_2^2\leq2$ gives a convex problem. Which statement about the two problems is correct?
options: The relaxed optimum is the centre $(0,0)$ of the disc, with $Z=0$, so the equality problem needs another method.
The relaxed problem is solved by $(1,1)$ with $Z=2$, a point of the circle, which therefore solves the equality problem too.
The relaxed optimum $(-1,-1)$, with $Z=-2$, lies on the circle, so it is also optimal for the equality problem.
The relaxation always has the same optimal solutions as the equality problem, so the original is convex too.
